title: On-time flights: a decision rule, its errors and their consequences

stimulus.title: Checking an airline's on-time claim
stimulus.html:
An airline advertises that 90% of its flights arrive on time. A consumer group will file a formal complaint if it finds convincing evidence that fewer than 90% of the airline's flights arrive on time. The group selects a random sample of 150 of the airline's thousands of flights from last month and records whether each arrived on time. The group's rule: file the complaint if 128 or fewer of the 150 flights arrived on time.

The group's plan
ItemValue
Advertised on-time proportion0.90
Flights sampled150, chosen at random
Decision rulecomplain if 128 or fewer arrived on time

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Suppose the airline's claim is true. Let XX be the number of the 150 sampled flights that arrive on time. Identify the distribution of XX, with its parameters, and calculate P(X≤128)P(X \le 128).

rubric.point: Identifies X as binomial with n = 150 and p = 0.90, with X defined in context (the number of sampled flights that arrive on time)
accept: X ~ binomial(n = 150, p = 0.9)
binomial, 150 trials, success = on time, probability 0.90

rubric.point: Calculates P(X <= 128) = 0.044, showing the boundary and direction (the sum of binomial probabilities for 0 to 128, or a cumulative binomial command named in words)
accept: binomcdf with n = 150, p = 0.9, up to 128, described in words, giving 0.044
P(X = 128) or P(X < 128) = 0.0256 does not earn this point

parts.sample: X = the number of the 150 sampled flights that arrive on time. If the claim is true, X is binomial with n = 150 and p = 0.90 (the sample is less than 10% of the airline's flights, so the trials are close to independent). P(X <= 128) = P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) + ... + P(X = 128) = 0.0440, from a cumulative binomial calculation with n = 150, p = 0.9, up to 128.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The group's rule is a significance test. Identify the null and alternative hypotheses, defining the parameter.

rubric.point: H_0: p = 0.90 and H_a: p < 0.90, where p is the true proportion of all the airline's flights (last month) that arrive on time
accept: H_0: p = 0.9, H_a: p < 0.9, p = the proportion of all the airline's flights that are on time
hypotheses written about p-hat, or with no parameter defined, do not earn this point

parts.sample: H_0: p = 0.90 and H_a: p < 0.90, where p = the true proportion of all the airline's flights last month that arrived on time.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Describe a Type I error in the context of this study, and explain one consequence of making it.

rubric.point: Type I error in context with the condition: the true proportion of all the airline's flights that arrive on time is 0.90, but the group finds convincing evidence that it is less than 0.90 (and files the complaint)
accept: the airline really does have 90% on time, but 128 or fewer of the sampled flights are on time and the group complains
a description without the condition that H_0 is true does not earn this point

rubric.point: A consequence that follows from the Type I error, in context
accept: the airline is accused unfairly and may lose customers or spend money answering a complaint it did not deserve
the group wastes time and credibility on a false complaint

parts.sample: A Type I error would occur if the true proportion of all the airline's flights that arrive on time is 0.90, but the group finds convincing evidence that it is less than 0.90 and files the complaint. The airline would be accused unfairly and could lose customers over a claim that was true.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Describe a Type II error in the context of this study, and explain one consequence of making it.

rubric.point: Type II error in context with the condition: the true proportion of all the airline's flights that arrive on time is less than 0.90, but the group does not find convincing evidence of it (and files no complaint)
accept: fewer than 90% of the airline's flights are really on time, but more than 128 of the sampled flights are on time, so the group does not complain
a description that says the group "accepts" that the claim is true is not penalized for the error type, but must include the condition

rubric.point: A consequence that follows from the Type II error, in context
accept: the airline keeps advertising a misleading on-time rate and travelers keep choosing it on false information
passengers keep facing late flights with no complaint filed

parts.sample: A Type II error would occur if the true proportion of all the airline's flights that arrive on time is less than 0.90, but the group does not find convincing evidence that it is less than 0.90 and files no complaint. The airline would keep advertising a misleading on-time rate, and travelers would keep booking it based on a claim that is false.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Interpret the probability you calculated in part (a) in terms of the group's possible errors.

rubric.point: Identifies 0.044 as the probability of a Type I error for this decision rule: if 90% of flights really are on time, there is about a 4.4% chance the group files the complaint anyway
accept: P(Type I error) = 0.044
the chance of complaining when the airline's claim is true is 0.044

parts.sample: 0.044 is the probability of a Type I error with this rule: if 90% of all the airline's flights really are on time, there is about a 0.044 probability that 128 or fewer of the 150 sampled flights are on time, so the group would file a complaint that is not justified.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: The group wants a smaller probability of a Type II error without raising the probability of a Type I error. Explain how it could change its study to do this, and why the change works.

rubric.point: Proposes a larger random sample of flights (with a cutoff chosen to keep the Type I error probability about the same)
accept: sample more than 150 flights
increase the sample size; changing alpha alone does not earn this point, because it raises the Type I error probability

rubric.point: Explains why: with a larger sample, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion is less variable, so the distributions under H_0 and under a true rate below 0.90 overlap less; power increases and the probability of a Type II error decreases
accept: a larger n gives a smaller standard deviation of p-hat, so a real shortfall is easier to detect
more power against any true proportion below 0.90

parts.sample: Take a larger random sample of flights, say 400, and set the cutoff so the probability of a Type I error stays about 0.044. With a larger sample the sample proportion varies less from sample to sample, so the sampling distribution when 90% are on time and the one when, say, 85% are on time overlap less. The test is then more likely to detect a real shortfall: its power goes up and the probability of a Type II error goes down.
